Guests
gĕsts
n. pl. (those invited to a table; in Scripture, the invited of a feast whose host determines everything)
Old Norse gestr, a guest, cognate with Latin hostis. In the Authorized Version the guests are always defined by the host who bade them.

Biblical Definition

Adonijah's coronation feast at Enrogel is the first scene: “Adonijah and all the guests that were with him heard it as they had made an end of eating” (1Ki 1:41), and when the news came that Solomon had been anointed at Gihon, “all the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and went every man his way” (1Ki 1:49). A table full of men committed to a usurper emptied in a moment when the true king was crowned. The second is Wisdom's rival: the foolish woman has her own house, her own table, and her own invitation, Stolen waters are sweet — “But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell” (Pro 9:18). Two houses, two suppers, two guest lists, and Proverbs 9 sets them side by side on purpose. The third is Zephaniah: “Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD: for the day of the LORD is at hand: for the LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests” (Zep 1:7) — and in that terrible passage the guests are invited to a sacrifice in which Judah is the victim. Scripture's last word on the subject is the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the beatitude attached: Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a guest as a stranger or friend entertained in the house or at the table of another; a visitor; one who is entertained.

expand to see more

GUEST, n. A stranger or friend entertained in the house or at the table of another, whether by invitation or otherwise; a visitor.

2. A stranger or person who lodges at an inn or tavern.

The LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests. Zeph. i.

Key Scripture

1Ki 1:49 — "And all the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and went every man his way."

Pro 9:18 — "But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell."

Zep 1:7 — "Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD: for the day of the LORD is at hand: for the LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests."

Modern Corruption

Both houses in Proverbs 9 send out the same invitation in the same words, and a generation trained to choose by preference has no way to tell them apart.

expand to see more

Proverbs 9 is built as a deliberate pair, and the symmetry is the whole point. Wisdom has builded her house, hewn out her seven pillars, killed her beasts, mingled her wine, furnished her table, and sent forth her maidens to cry upon the highest places of the city. The foolish woman is clamorous, simple, and knoweth nothing, and she sits at the door of her house on a seat in the high places of the city. Then they both call, and the words are identical: Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither. The invitations are indistinguishable by their form. Only the outcomes differ — forsake the foolish, and live, on the one hand; her guests are in the depths of hell, on the other. That is a devastating passage for an age which chooses its beliefs, its companions and its loves by the appeal of the invitation, and which has been taught that the authentic desire of the heart is the most reliable guide available. Proverbs answers that the desire is exactly what is being competed for, that both callers know it, and that both will offer sweetness. The chapter gives one instrument of discrimination and one only, and it is verse 10: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Adonijah's guests found out the same thing more cheaply than most — they discovered whose table they were at only when the trumpet sounded for the true king.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qara' (H7121), to call, to invite; qaruw', the called ones, the bidden guests; Greek kletos (G2822), called, invited — the word behind the marriage supper.

expand to see more

Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call, to summon, to invite; the LORD bidding His guests to the sacrifice; Zephaniah 1:7, 1 Samuel 9:13.

Hebrew rapha'iym (H7496) — the dead, the shades; who are in the house of the foolish woman without the guests' knowledge; Proverbs 9:18, 2:18.

Greek kletos (G2822) — called, invited; the many called and the few chosen, and the blessed who are called to the marriage supper; Matthew 22:14, Revelation 19:9.

Usage

"“All the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid” — a usurper's table emptied by a trumpet."

"“Her guests are in the depths of hell” — the other house in Proverbs 9, with the same invitation."

"“He hath bid his guests” — a sacrifice in which the nation is the victim."
